title: Networking foundations

sources.title: The OSI Model
sources.scope: Read overview and layer descriptions: seven-layer conceptual troubleshooting model, including functions of application through physical layers; modern Internet does not strictly map to OSI.

sources.title: RFC 791: Internet Protocol
sources.scope: Read abstract and introductory IP operation material on connectionless datagrams, addressing, routing and gateways.

sources.title: RFC 8200: IPv6 Specification
sources.scope: Read specification overview and IPv6 addressing/header material; grounds IPv6 protocol facts.

sources.title: RFC 4632: Classless Inter-domain Routing
sources.scope: Read abstract and prefix notation sections: explicit prefix lengths and classless address assignment/aggregation.

sources.title: Configure IP Addresses and Unique Subnets
sources.scope: Read IP/subnet definitions, dotted decimal explanation and subnet examples; older tutorial, classful assumptions are historical only.

sources.title: NIST Definition of Cloud Computing
sources.scope: Read NIST SP 800-145 abstract and definition: on-demand shared configurable resources, rapid provisioning/release, measured service and IaaS/PaaS/SaaS models.

sources.title: 5G System Overview
sources.scope: Read 3GPP introduction, system architecture and service descriptions: UE, radio access network and core; eMBB, massive IoT and critical/URLLC goals. Goals are not universal service guarantees.

sources.title: IEEE 802.11 Working Group
sources.scope: Read working-group scope describing WLAN MAC and PHY standardization; this does not support universal range or throughput figures.

pages.title: LAN scale and purpose
notes: A LAN connects devices within a limited local site.
It lets endpoints share links, services and local resources.
A switch forwards Ethernet frames using learned MAC locations.
A router forwards IP packets between separate IP networks.
Layer 2 means link-local framing; Layer 3 means IP routing.
An ordinary Layer 2 switch forwards within its VLAN.
A Layer 3 switch can also route between configured networks.
VLANs do not encrypt traffic or prevent all access.
LAN ownership and management depend on the organization.

pages.title: SOHO, enterprise and datacenter
notes: SOHO means small office/home office, usually few users.
An integrated gateway may combine router, Wi-Fi and switching.
Integration saves cost but limits capacity and redundancy.
Enterprise LANs use managed access across campuses.
VLANs and routed boundaries organize traffic and policy.
Central management spreads both settings and errors.
Datacenter LANs connect dense server and storage systems.
Redundant links can improve availability but add complexity.
No LAN guarantees speed, security or uninterrupted service.
Select scale by users, traffic, growth, support and budget.

pages.title: Encapsulation across a connection
notes: An application creates data for another host or service.
Transport adds headers to form segments or datagrams.
IP adds source and destination addresses in a packet.
The link layer wraps that packet in a local-link frame.
The physical layer transmits frame bits as signals.
The receiver processes headers in reverse order.
Each hop uses link delivery for the next local destination.
A router removes incoming frame and forwards the IP packet.
It builds a new frame appropriate to the outgoing link.

pages.title: Switch and router forwarding
notes: A Layer 2 switch consults its MAC forwarding table.
Unknown unicast may be flooded within the eligible VLAN.
A router examines IP destination and selects a next hop.
Routers separate broadcast domains by default.
A Layer 3 switch can perform routing when configured to do so.
Only ordinary Layer 2 switch operation does not route.
A next hop may be another router, not the destination.
Link rate is not payload throughput because of overhead.
Filtering policy is separate from basic forwarding.
Congestion, link failures and bad routes can cause loss.

practice.prompt: Trace a browser request to a remote server and explain what a router changes.
practice.answer: Transport and IP headers are carried inside a local-link frame. The router removes the incoming link framing, chooses a next hop by IP routing, and sends the packet in a new outgoing-link frame; link MAC delivery changes hop by hop.

practice.prompt: Does a switch always mean it cannot route between subnets?
practice.answer: No. An ordinary Layer 2 switch forwards frames within its VLAN, but a Layer 3 switch can route between configured networks. The device label alone does not specify enabled functions.

pages.title: OSI: physical and data link
notes: OSI is a seven-layer model, not a product blueprint.
Layer 1 sends bits as electrical, optical or radio signals.
It defines media, signaling and connection properties.
Copper, fiber and radio differ in reach and noise limits.
Layer 2 data link groups bits into frames on a local link.
Ethernet and Wi-Fi link delivery use link-layer addressing.
Switches learn source MAC locations and forward frames.
Frames are link-local; routers reframe packets for each link.
Errors, shared-media collisions or loops disrupt delivery.

pages.title: OSI: network through application
notes: Layer 3 network moves packets between networks using IP.
Routers choose next hops using destination and routing data.
Layer 4 carries process traffic using ports and protocols.
TCP offers ordered delivery and retransmits lost data.
UDP provides datagrams without TCP's delivery guarantees.
Layer 5 organizes dialogs between communicating systems.
Layer 6 presentation represents, encodes or transforms data.
Layer 7 protocols support tasks such as web requests.
Internet protocols do not always fit one OSI layer exactly.
OSI aids troubleshooting; it is not a wire-level recipe.

pages.title: Network troubleshooting model
notes: OSI layers provide a shared vocabulary for fault isolation.
No link signal suggests checking power, cable or interface.
A local link can work while IP addressing or routing is wrong.
Transport failure may affect a particular service or port.
Application failure may persist despite working lower layers.
Layer symptoms are clues, not proof of a single cause.
Modern protocol stacks combine functions differently from OSI.
Check end-to-end behavior after repairing a local symptom.
Do not infer security from a device's OSI layer alone.

pages.title: LAN design in context
notes: A small shop may use a compact gateway and switched LAN.
A campus commonly uses managed access and routed boundaries.
Datacenter design focuses on server and storage traffic paths.
Capacity planning considers concurrent users and traffic.
Redundant equipment may share power or cable risks.
Segmentation constrains traffic only with correct policy.
More bandwidth cannot fix a wrong route or weak Wi-Fi.
Skills and maintenance matter alongside equipment cost.
Choose components for the site's actual availability needs.
Document dependencies so outages can be diagnosed efficiently.

practice.prompt: How does encapsulation change at a router?
practice.answer: A router removes incoming link framing, forwards the IP packet by destination, and creates new framing for the outgoing link.

practice.prompt: Can any switch route between subnets?
practice.answer: No. Ordinary Layer 2 switches forward frames within a VLAN; Layer 3 switches can route when configured.

pages.title: From device to ISP
notes: A network adapter connects a device to a wired or radio link.
A switch or access point joins devices to the local LAN.
A router joins IP networks and selects a route toward the ISP.
A modem adapts signaling for a provider medium such as coax.
An optical network terminal adapts a fiber access connection.
A gateway may combine modem, routing, switching and Wi-Fi.
The ISP aggregates access and routes to other networks.
Operators interconnect through peering or paid transit.
Available access media depend on the local provider.

pages.title: ISP chain and local limits
notes: A home link does not directly cable to every Internet host.
Traffic crosses local gear, then provider networks.
Fiber, coax, DSL and cellular differ in signaling and reach.
The provider medium and plan constrain the access link rate.
A live physical link does not prove DNS or routing is working.
A reachable router does not prove remote service works.
Power or ISP faults can interrupt a correctly addressed LAN.
Speed tests include remote path and server limitations.
Check link, route, DNS and remote service separately.
One device may combine modem and router functions.

pages.title: IPv4 and IPv6 formats
notes: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, commonly shown as four octets.
Each dotted-decimal octet ranges from 0 through 255.
IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as hexadecimal groups.
IPv6 uses colons; :: can compress one run of zero groups.
IPv6 greatly expands available address space over IPv4.
IPv6 has a different header and uses Neighbor Discovery.
IPv4 commonly uses ARP on Ethernet links for local resolution.
Dual stack runs IPv4 and IPv6 together during transition.
IPv6 still needs suitable access policy and configuration.

pages.title: Subnet calculation example
notes: For 192.0.2.70/26, six bits remain for host positions.
A /26 block has 64 total addresses.
The aligned block containing .70 starts at 192.0.2.64.
The dotted mask is 255.255.255.192.
Under ordinary LAN convention, .64 is the network address.
The corresponding broadcast address is 192.0.2.127.
Ordinary assignable range is 192.0.2.65 through .126.
State the address-use convention when describing host range.
A /32 denotes one IPv4 address route, not a LAN subnet.
A /31 is a point-to-point exception to ordinary host rules.

practice.prompt: Calculate the network and ordinary LAN usable range for 192.0.2.70/26.
practice.answer: The block has 64 addresses and begins at .64. Mask is 255.255.255.192; ordinary LAN convention treats .64 as network and .127 as broadcast, leaving .65-.126. A /31 point-to-point link is a defined exception.

practice.prompt: Why are Class A/B/C masks not used to determine a modern prefix?
practice.answer: CIDR uses an explicitly configured prefix length and classless allocation. Historical classes are useful as history, but the address's first octet does not determine its current subnet mask.

sheets.title: IP formats, CIDR and subnet calculation

pages.title: IP and MAC addressing
notes: IP addresses identify interfaces for logical packet delivery.
Routers compare destination IP with network prefixes to route.
MAC addresses identify link-layer interfaces on a local link.
Switches learn source MAC locations to forward local frames.
A router uses a new link frame at each routed hop.
MAC is not the end-to-end Internet destination address.
Address resolution finds a local link address for a next hop.
IP and MAC values alone do not prove identity or permission.
Addresses may be assigned manually or by network services.

pages.title: Subnet purpose and CIDR
notes: A subnet groups addresses sharing a common network prefix.
Subnetting divides blocks for routing and administration.
CIDR writes a prefix length, such as IPv4 /24.
A /24 means 24 leading bits identify the IPv4 prefix.
Its dotted mask is 255.255.255.0; mask bits are contiguous.
IPv4 block size is 2^(32 minus prefix length) addresses.
Network boundaries align to the block size.
CIDR uses explicit prefixes, not inferred address classes.
Subnet design balances growth, address use and broadcasts.
A /31 can assign both addresses on a point-to-point link.

pages.title: Historical IPv4 address classes
notes: Class A historically had first octet 1 through 126.
Class B historically had first octet 128 through 191.
Class C historically had first octet 192 through 223.
Class D: first octet 224-239; multicast addresses.
Class E: first octet 240-255; historically experimental.
Special-use values limit these simplified historical ranges.
Classful networks once implied default network masks.
Classless CIDR replaced class-based routing and allocation.
Modern configuration specifies a prefix or mask explicitly.

pages.title: Addressing and planning limits
notes: Size subnets for planned growth without needless waste.
Separate prefixes can simplify routing and management.
Subnetting alone does not block all inter-host traffic.
Routing policy determines which networks can exchange packets.
Plan IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and firewall rules separately.
Special-use ranges are not ordinary public host allocations.
Allocation and reachability depend on provider and setup.
Do not infer a modern prefix from historical class labels.
Verify mask, boundary and host rules for the specific link.
Legacy subnet tutorials may use simplified classful examples.

practice.prompt: Calculate 192.0.2.70/26 network and usable LAN range.
practice.answer: The aligned block is .64-.127 with mask 255.255.255.192; ordinary LAN hosts are .65-.126. /31 point-to-point is an exception.
CIDR uses an explicit prefix length; class labels do not determine modern masks.

pages.title: Peer-to-peer and client-server
notes: Peer-to-peer devices share resources directly with peers.
Two home computers sharing files are a simple P2P example.
Each peer manages its own resources and access decisions.
P2P avoids a dedicated server but peer availability varies.
Client-server assigns a service role to a server system.
Clients request service, such as files, from that server.
A file server can centralize permissions, storage and backup.
Central services need adequate capacity and recovery plans.
Both models need appropriate access and security controls.

pages.title: Choose a service architecture
notes: Small trusted groups may value P2P simplicity and low cost.
Growing organizations may need centrally managed services.
Server failure can affect many clients at once.
Replicated services may reduce but not eliminate dependencies.
P2P users can make inconsistent copies and permissions.
Server administration needs staffing, patching and monitoring.
Client-server describes service roles, not physical layout.
A server may be virtual or hosted outside the local LAN.
Select based on scale, access control, continuity and budget.
A central server still needs backup and restore testing.

pages.title: Star and bus topologies
notes: Star connects endpoints to a central switch or access point.
Adding a star endpoint is usually straightforward.
A central switch or uplink fault can disconnect many users.
Bus topology shares a common backbone among connected devices.
Legacy coax Ethernet used bus-like shared media.
A backbone break can interrupt service for many bus devices.
Shared medium can create contention as traffic grows.
Modern switched Ethernet generally uses physical star cabling.
Physical wiring layout and logical forwarding can differ.

pages.title: Ring and mesh topologies
notes: A ring links nodes in a closed path for traffic circulation.
A ring break can interrupt service without alternate paths.
A mesh provides multiple paths between selected network nodes.
Full mesh links every pair; partial mesh links chosen pairs.
Alternative paths can support resilience after a link failure.
More mesh links increase installation and routing complexity.
Wireless mesh relays traffic and consumes shared airtime.
Redundancy helps only when alternate paths are independent.
Loops require controls to prevent repeated frame circulation.
Capacity must support rerouted traffic after a failure.

practice.prompt: A clinic needs easy growth but less dependence on one uplink. What topology change could help?
practice.answer: A switched star is manageable but its central uplink is a failure point. Add an independently routed second uplink or selected mesh path if the cost and operations justify it; redundant paths sharing one conduit are not independent.

practice.prompt: Contrast P2P file sharing with a client-server file service for multiple branches.
practice.answer: P2P is decentralized with variable availability and separate permission management. Client-server centralizes access and backup, but depends on server capacity and WAN reachability for branches.

pages.title: LAN, MAN and WAN scope
notes: LAN means local area network across a limited site or campus.
A MAN spans a metropolitan or city region.
A WAN joins distant sites across larger geographic areas.
WAN links often depend on telecom or Internet providers.
Routers connect local networks across inter-site links.
Geographic scope does not specify ownership or a fixed speed.
WAN distance often increases latency and service cost.
Provider outages can affect several connected locations.
A VPN protects a path; it cannot prevent provider outages.

pages.title: WAN implications and scale
notes: A company WAN may link branches, headquarters and datacenters.
Applications sensitive to delay need realistic WAN testing.
Bandwidth and latency are distinct performance properties.
A MAN may be provider-operated or organization-managed.
LAN typically supports local switching and local services.
WAN agreements specify capacity and availability terms.
Backup circuits help only if routes and infrastructure differ.
A remote site still relies on its local LAN and gateway.
Choose scope from users, geography and application needs.
No topology name guarantees a particular reliability level.

pages.title: Choose topology for requirements
notes: A small office often uses a switched star for easy management.
A critical site may add diverse uplinks for availability.
A partial mesh trades extra paths against cost and complexity.
Legacy bus is rarely a new Ethernet installation choice.
Compare failure impact, growth, traffic and operator skills.
A central star switch is a possible single point of failure.
Separate power and physical routes improve path independence.
No topology is best for every business requirement.
Physical cabling choices also constrain speed and distance.

pages.title: Wireless network size options
notes: A small LAN may use an integrated Wi-Fi router or one AP.
An access point bridges wireless clients to a wired LAN.
Large campuses deploy multiple managed access points.
AP placement should account for coverage and client density.
Wired backhaul avoids radio retransmission at every hop.
Managed systems coordinate settings and may support roaming.
Cloud management adds provider and Internet dependencies.
Survey results vary with walls, interference and location.
More APs do not automatically create better coverage.
All network sizes need secure settings and monitoring.

practice.prompt: How can a clinic reduce a star uplink failure risk?
practice.answer: Add an independent uplink or partial mesh if cost and operations justify it; shared pathways are not independent.

practice.prompt: Why might campuses deploy managed access points?
practice.answer: Multiple managed APs provide planned coverage and capacity, but need backhaul, configuration and ongoing management.

pages.title: Cloud definition and service models
notes: Cloud offers on-demand access to shared computing resources.
Resources include networks, servers, storage and applications.
Cloud resources can be rapidly provisioned and released.
IaaS provides configurable compute, storage and networking.
IaaS customers usually manage guest systems and applications.
PaaS supplies a platform for customers to deploy applications.
PaaS provider manages more underlying runtime infrastructure.
SaaS delivers a provider-operated application to its users.
Service models distinguish provider and customer control.

pages.title: Service model use and responsibility
notes: IaaS suits teams needing control of virtual machines.
PaaS runs customer code on a provider-managed platform.
SaaS suits organizations using a finished hosted application.
Provider duties differ by service and contract.
Customers still manage identities, access and data use.
Shared responsibility does not remove customer duties.
A hosted service depends on its provider and network path.
Clarify backup, retention and recovery terms before adoption.
Cloud describes a delivery model, not one physical location.
Service boundaries vary, so verify the actual offer terms.

pages.title: Radio frequency and attenuation
notes: Radio frequency (RF) carries wireless signals through space.
Distance generally weakens received signal strength.
Walls and building materials absorb or reflect radio energy.
Metal and reinforced concrete can obstruct or reflect signals.
Interference and noise can corrupt reception or cut capacity.
A client and access point both need adequate signal quality.
A strong signal does not guarantee a fast Internet connection.
Range depends on frequency, antenna, power and environment.
No single indoor Wi-Fi range applies to every building.

pages.title: Wireless speed and reliability
notes: Wi-Fi PHY rate is a signaling maximum, not app throughput.
Overhead and retransmissions reduce usable throughput.
Congestion shares airtime among nearby clients.
Channel width and modulation affect capacity and reach.
Client capability can limit an AP's advertised link rate.
Backhaul capacity can bottleneck otherwise strong Wi-Fi.
Roaming, power and configuration affect reliability.
Survey at actual user locations and test representative load.
Higher AP power may not strengthen a client's return signal.
Band, regulation and hardware determine available channels.

practice.prompt: A company selects hosted email. Identify the cloud model and two retained concerns.
practice.answer: Hosted email is SaaS because the provider delivers the application. The customer still manages user access and data decisions, and should confirm recovery and retention responsibilities; service terms define the boundary.

practice.prompt: Why might a 5G user near a window have different service than indoors?
practice.answer: Radio band, distance, building attenuation, spectrum and local cell deployment affect reception. 5G service categories describe system goals, not guaranteed end-to-end performance at every location.

pages.title: Cloud benefits and operating costs
notes: On-demand provisioning can shorten deployment time.
Elastic resources can scale with changing workload demand.
Measured service ties some costs to consumption.
Less local hardware can reduce some maintenance work.
Usage charges, licenses and support create ongoing costs.
Data transfer and storage can add to monthly bills.
Migration and staff learning require time and resources.
Variable demand can make costs difficult to forecast.
Cloud is not automatically cheaper than local infrastructure.

pages.title: Cloud risks and planning
notes: Provider outages can make hosted services unavailable.
Misconfigured permissions can expose data or resources.
Provider dependence can make migration or exit difficult.
Location and retention of data affect compliance obligations.
Plan access controls and recovery responsibilities in advance.
Assess portability and export options before committing.
Use budgets and alerts to monitor measured consumption.
Provider safeguards do not replace correct customer setup.
Availability depends on app, network and provider systems.
Compare risks and costs with the business continuity need.

pages.title: Wireless LAN and cellular options
notes: IEEE 802.11 defines WLAN medium access and physical layers.
Wi-Fi commonly links local devices through access points.
Cellular networks provide operator-managed wide-area mobility.
Wi-Fi generally uses local access points and backhaul.
Unlicensed Wi-Fi bands can be crowded by neighboring networks.
Cellular coverage depends on operator deployment and spectrum.
Large campus Wi-Fi requires placement and capacity planning.
Small networks may use a single integrated wireless gateway.
Neither Wi-Fi nor cellular has one universal speed or range.

pages.title: 5G system and service families
notes: 5G is a 3GPP mobile system, not a single radio frequency.
A 5G system includes user equipment, radio access and core.
5G New Radio (NR) is the radio interface family.
Enhanced mobile broadband targets high data-rate services.
Massive IoT targets communication for many connected devices.
Critical communications target reliability and low latency.
Network slicing can tailor logical network capabilities.
Service goals depend on deployment and end-to-end path.
Low latency is not guaranteed for every 5G application.
Spectrum, obstacles and distance affect coverage and capacity.

practice.prompt: Why can Wi-Fi signal be strong but throughput poor?
practice.answer: Congestion, protocol overhead, client limits or backhaul bottlenecks can reduce throughput despite signal strength.

practice.prompt: What are 5G service families intended to support?
practice.answer: eMBB targets data rates, massive IoT many devices, and critical/URLLC services reliability and latency goals; these are not guarantees.

lab.title: Safe local Wi-Fi observation
steps: Predict which of two authorized indoor locations has weaker Wi-Fi and explain why.
Using only a network you are authorized to use, record the signal indicator and one ordinary download result at each location.
Repeat at a different time and discuss walls, congestion, device limits and Internet path as possible causes.
expected: Results may show a location difference but cannot isolate its cause.
Signal bars and a single speed test do not establish universal range or throughput.
No traffic capture, credential collection or network configuration change is needed.

limitations: OSI is a conceptual model; real Internet protocols do not map perfectly to seven discrete layers.
Historical IPv4 class ranges are simplified and must not be used to infer modern CIDR prefixes.
Wireless range and 5G performance depend on local environment, hardware, regulation and deployment.
